claim: CSR provides direct experimental evidence that verbalized confidence under RLCR is unstable at three levels: the decoded confidence token itself has high entropy for a single sample, multiple generations that give the same final answer report inconsistent confidence values, and confidence still varies widely within a semantic-equivalence group.
stance_target: verbalized confidence tokens are a stable/reliable readout of model uncertainty
scope_conditions: RLCR-trained models on HotpotQA and OOD QA datasets
quoted_support: Panel (a) shows that even for a single sampled answer, the decoded confidence is not a stable quantity: alternative values appear in the output distribution with substantial probability. Panel (b) shows that multiple responses producing the same answer report inconsistent confidence scores.

claim: CSR concludes that existing verbalized-confidence RL methods 'calibrate a reporting interface rather than the model's underlying uncertainty over answer meanings,' and therefore proposes bypassing the verbalized interface entirely in favor of semantic-cluster-space calibration.
stance_target: training a verbalized confidence interface is the right approach to expressed calibration
quoted_support: In this work, we propose to calibrate language models directly in semantic space, bypassing the verbalized confidence interface.

claim: CSR documents practical format-parsing failure rates for verbalized-confidence baselines RD (Rewarding Doubt) and RLCR, which require outputs to conform to a specific reporting format -- a concrete deployment cost of the verbalized-interface approach.
stance_target: verbalized confidence interfaces are practically reliable to deploy
quoted_support: To assess the practical reliability of verbalized-confidence methods, we examine parsing failures and format-error rates for RD and RLCR, which require outputs to conform to a specific format.

claim: CSR was fine-tuned with 4-bit LoRA (rank 32, alpha 32, 7 modules) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Mistral, with each individual training or evaluation run using a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU.
stance_target: single-GPU 7-8B feasibility of calibration-aware RL training
quoted_support: Each individual fine-tuning or evaluation run uses a single A100 80GB GPU... models are loaded in 4-bit precision and fine-tuned with LoRA adapters using rank 32 and alpha 32, applied to 7 modules.

claim: CSR reduces ECE by up to 42% and improves AUROC by up to 31% relative to verbalized-confidence baselines (RD, RLCR) across three model families and four QA datasets, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution datasets (TriviaQA, MSMARCO, NQ-Open).
stance_target: non-verbalized/semantic calibration outperforms verbalized calibration on standard QA
quoted_support: CSR achieves the lowest ECE and highest AUROC in nearly every cell at a token cost comparable to the base model.

claim: An ablation shows a calibration-only reward (no correctness term) achieves very high AUROC but collapses task accuracy, while correctness-only RLVR yields only moderate AUROC gains -- demonstrating that discrimination and accuracy pull in different directions unless a joint objective is used.
stance_target: discrimination and task accuracy require an explicitly joint training objective, not either reward alone
quoted_support: The calibration reward alone achieves very high AUROC but collapses accuracy, indicating that semantic calibration in isolation can produce separable confidence scores without preserving correctness.

claim: CSR is evaluated exclusively on open-ended QA datasets (HotpotQA, TriviaQA, MSMARCO, NQ-Open) and never on math or code benchmarks, leaving code-domain calibration entirely untested by this method.
stance_target: prior calibration-aware RL work leaves a code-domain gap
quoted_support: Experiments across three model families on HotpotQA (in-distribution) and TriviaQA, MSMARCO, and NQ-Open (out-of-distribution) show that CSR consistently achieves lower ECE and higher AUROC than verbalized-confidence baselines.
